title: SRE playbook generator and actionable metrics cookbook
author: Sofia Alvarez
body:
Overview

This document describes the design patterns, templates, and operational guidance for the SRE Playbook Generator: a lightweight tooling and process cookbook that turns observed telemetry signals into concise, actionable runbook steps. The goal is to reduce cognitive load during incidents by providing pre-approved, signal-driven playbook fragments and a clear mapping from metric state to operator action.

Why we need this

- Modern inference workloads produce many correlated signals (latency tails, token-level error spikes, queue depth).
- On-call responders need short, deterministic actions rather than long narrative runbooks.
- Automated playbook suggestions help junior responders and speed mean-time-to-recovery (MTTR) while preserving change controls.

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: SLO-related signals (latency/availability/error budget burn), capacity indicators (queueing, GPU utilization, OOMs), and degradation patterns (quantized tail latencies, KV cache miss storms).
- Non-goal: Full incident automation. Generator produces human-reviewed suggestions; execution requires human acknowledgment or an approved automation policy.

Key concepts

1) Actionable metric: a metric with a defined trigger, severity tier, and a single short remediation action. Example: "p99 token latency > 2.5s for 10m" -> severity=severe -> action=route-to-fallback-model.

2) Signal-to-action mapping: deterministic mapping stored as YAML rules consumed by the generator. Rules are scoped by service, SLO name, and telemetry source.

3) Playbook fragment: a 2–4 line actionable instruction with ownership, single-command diagnostics, and safe rollback notes. Fragments must be pre-approved by service owner.

Design of the Playbook Generator

- Input: Event stream (alerts, metric windows, tracing anomalies) + service config (SLO thresholds, owner, allowed mitigations).
- Engine: rule matcher that evaluates signal rules in priority order, deduplicates overlapping rules, and outputs ranked fragments.
- Output: Compact incident card with: title, severity, matched signals, recommended fragments, single-line CLI commands, and owner/team contact.

Rule sample (YAML fragment)

service: text-generation
rule_id: p99_latency_route_fallback
severity: high
match: |
  metrics.p99_latency > 2.5 and window >= 600
action: |
  - fragment_id: route-fallback-2
  - reason: p99 above threshold; potential model load or KV-cache miss
priority: 100
approved_by: "service-owner@redwood.com"

Playbook fragment template (YAML)

fragment_id: route-fallback-2
description: "Switch traffic for low-latency tenants to fallback model v2-quantized for up to 30m"
action_steps:
  - "Identify top 3 impacted tenants: curl http://telemetry/services/text-generation/top-tenants?window=10m"
  - "Execute routing change: rhctl traffic route --service text-generation --from model-v3 --to model-v2-fallback --weight 25"
  - "Monitor p99 latency and error rate for 5 minutes"
rollback: "rhctl traffic route --service text-generation --from model-v2-fallback --to model-v3 --weight 100"
owner: "team-runtime"
preconditions: "fallback model v2-fallback in healthy state (healthcheck: /healthz returns 200)"

Example SLO mapping table

| SLO name | Target | Alert threshold | Playbook fragment | Owner | Capacity trigger |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---:|
| text-gen-availability | 99.95% | 99.7% over 30m | fragment-id: availability-hedge | team-runtime | queue-depth > 1200 |
| embedding-p99 | 800ms | 1.2s over 10m | fragment-id: route-fallback-2 | team-embeddings | GPU-util > 91% |

Operational runbook: triage flow (condensed)

1) Ingest
  - On alert, the generated incident card is posted to #oncall-incident and to the incident channel in PagerDuty.
2) Rapid assessment (first 5 minutes)
  - Confirm signal sources (metrics, traces, errors).
  - Accept or reject each suggested fragment (click "apply" in console or run the one-line CLI).
3) Execute safe mitigations (5–20 minutes)
  - Apply 1 mitigation at a time; wait 5 minutes for telemetry to stabilize.
  - If severity increases, escalate to the escalation playbook.
4) Stabilize & recovery
  - After visible improvement, run validation checks (synthetic canaries, per-tenant latency).
  - Schedule follow-up actions: capacity provisioning, model rollback, root-cause investigation.

CLI examples

- Generate suggestions from local snapshot:
  redwood-sre-generator suggest --service text-generation --snapshot /tmp/sample.json --output incident-card.json

- Apply a fragment (requires approval token):
  redwood-sre-generator apply --fragment route-fallback-2 --incident-id INC12345 --approver tok_xxx

Operational safety controls

- All fragments must include explicit preconditions and rollback commands.
- "Apply" requires either on-call approval (manual click) or a signed automation policy (stored in Vault).
- Rate limits: no fragment may increase traffic to a different model by more than 40% without SRE lead approval.

Incident review evidence checklist

- Record matched rules and generator output JSON.
- Snapshot metric windows (start/end, p50/p95/p99, error-rate).
- Attach relevant traces and tenant identifiers.
- Document which fragments were applied, by whom, and command history (CLI audit).

Runbook maintenance and governance

- Owners must review fragments quarterly or when a model/route changes.
- A central fragment registry enforces naming, schema validation, and approval metadata.
- Annual tabletop: run the generator against recorded incidents and score suggested fragment relevance.

Capacity planning tie-ins

- Use generator output frequency as a demand signal: frequent suggestions for routing->fallback indicate under-provisioned headroom.
- Aggregate fragment application counts by tenant and dimension to inform reserved capacity proposals.

Rollout plan for the generator

1) Alpha (team-runtime only) — ingest 2 services, manual apply, 2-week pilot.
2) Beta (select services) — add approval gating, record metrics, expand to SRE oncall rotation.
3) GA — console integration, PagerDuty cards, and audit logging to SIEM.
